questions.prompt: A particle’s position is s(t)=t³−6t²+9t meters, with t in seconds. Which pair is (velocity, speed) at t=2?
questions.explanation: Differentiate position: v(t)=3t²−12t+9. At 2 this gives 12−24+9=−3 m/s. The speed is |v(2)|=3 m/s. The negative velocity identifies motion in the negative coordinate direction. A: This loses the negative sign of the velocity. B: Speed cannot be negative. C: Velocity is the signed derivative; speed is its absolute value. D: This substitutes the position value s(2)=2 for a rate.

questions.prompt: A particle has position s(t)=t⁴−4t² meters, with t in seconds. What is its acceleration at t=1?
questions.explanation: Velocity is v=s′=4t³−8t, and acceleration is a=v′=12t²−8. At t=1 the acceleration is 12−8=4 m/s². Its units are position divided by time squared. A: This is the numerical velocity value at 1, relabeled as acceleration. B: This is the numerical position value at 1. C: This omits the second derivative −8 of the quadratic term. D: Twice differentiating gives a(t)=12t²−8.

questions.prompt: For t≥0, a particle has velocity v(t)=t²−4t+3 meters per second. On which interval is it moving in the negative direction?
questions.explanation: Negative-direction motion requires v(t)<0. The factors t−1 and t−3 have opposite signs only for 1<t<3. At the endpoints the particle is at rest, so they are excluded. A: Factoring v=(t−1)(t−3) gives a negative product exactly between its roots. B: Both factors are negative there, so velocity is positive. C: Both factors are positive there, so velocity is positive. D: The sign of the polynomial is not negative throughout the time domain.

questions.prompt: At an instant, a particle moving along a line has velocity −4 m/s and acceleration −2 m/s². Which statement is correct?
options: It moves in the negative direction and slows down at 2 m/s².
It moves in the negative direction and its speed is increasing at 2 m/s².
It moves in the positive direction because its speed is 4 m/s.
Its speed is −4 m/s and decreases at 2 m/s².
questions.explanation: Velocity −4 means negative-direction motion. Since velocity is nonzero, the local speed derivative is sign(v)a=(−1)(−2)=2 m/s². Thus the particle is speeding up while moving in the negative direction. A: Velocity and acceleration have the same sign, so the speed is increasing. B: With negative velocity, speed is −v locally, so its derivative is −a=2. C: Speed has no direction; the negative velocity specifies direction. D: Speed is the nonnegative magnitude of velocity.

questions.prompt: A particle has velocity v(t)=4t−8 m/s for 0≤t≤3 s. When does it change direction?
options: At t=0 s, because observation begins there.
At t=1 s, because velocity is −4 m/s.
At t=2 s, because velocity changes from negative to positive.
Never, because acceleration is the constant 4 m/s².
questions.explanation: Solve v(t)=0 to get t=2. For times just before 2 the velocity is negative; just after 2 it is positive. This sign change establishes a change of direction. Constant acceleration does not prevent a reversal. A: Starting the recorded interval does not establish a direction reversal. B: A negative velocity value by itself is not a reversal. C: The zero at 2 separates opposite-sign velocity intervals. D: Constant positive acceleration can carry velocity through zero.

questions.prompt: A particle has velocity v(t)=(t−2)² m/s near t=2 s. Which statement is correct?
options: It changes direction because every zero of velocity is a reversal.
It is never at rest because a square is always strictly positive.
It moves in the negative direction immediately before 2 s.
It is momentarily at rest at 2 s but does not change direction there.
questions.explanation: The square gives v(2)=0, so the particle is at rest at that instant. For t≠2 sufficiently near 2, (t−2)²>0 on both sides. Thus there is no direction change despite the zero velocity. A: A sign change, not merely a zero value, is required. B: The square equals zero at its base zero. C: The squared quantity is positive before 2 as well as after it. D: Velocity is zero at 2 and positive on both sides.

questions.prompt: The graph below shows velocity v(t) in m/s versus time t in seconds. What is the acceleration at t=1 s?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is v′(t), the slope of the velocity graph. Time 1 lies inside the segment from (0,−2) to (2,2), so a(1)=[2−(−2)]/(2−0)=2 m/s². Zero velocity at that instant does not imply zero acceleration. A: Acceleration is the local graph slope (2−(−2))/(2−0). B: This uses the velocity height v(1)=0 instead of its slope. C: This uses the velocity rise without dividing by the 2-second run. D: This confuses the initial velocity height with acceleration.

questions.prompt: Use the velocity table below. Which value best estimates acceleration at t=2 s using a centered secant over the nearest displayed times on either side?
questions.explanation: The nearest displayed times on either side of 2 are 1 and 3. The centered secant estimate is a(2)≈[4−(−3)]/(3−1)=7/2=3.5 m/s². The finite table alone does not establish an exact derivative. A: This omits division by the 2-second time gap. B: Use [v(3)−v(1)]/(3−1)=[4−(−3)]/2. C: This is the velocity at t=2, not its rate of change. D: This is only the forward secant from 2 to 3, not the requested centered estimate.

questions.prompt: A particle has position s(t)=e^(−t) meters for t≥0, with time in seconds. Which description is correct just after t=0?
options: It moves in the positive direction and speeds up.
It moves in the negative direction and speeds up.
It moves in the negative direction and slows down.
It is at rest because position is approaching zero.
questions.explanation: Differentiate position to obtain v=−e^(−t) and a=e^(−t). Thus the particle moves toward decreasing position while its speed |v|=e^(−t) decreases. A positive position does not imply positive-direction motion. A: Position is positive, but direction depends on its negative derivative. B: Opposite signs of nonzero velocity and acceleration make speed decrease. C: Velocity is −e^(−t)<0 while acceleration is e^(−t)>0, so speed decreases. D: Velocity is nonzero at every finite time.

questions.prompt: A particle has position s(t)=t³−3t meters on 0≤t≤2 seconds. What total distance does it travel on this interval?
questions.explanation: Velocity is 3t²−3, negative on (0,1) and positive on (1,2), with one reversal at 1. Positions are s(0)=0, s(1)=−2 and s(2)=2. Total distance is |−2−0|+|2−(−2)|=2+4=6 m, whereas net displacement is 2 m. A: This is the net displacement, which cancels motion in opposite directions. B: This counts only the motion after the turn. C: Returning through the starting position does not erase traveled distance. D: It moves from position 0 to −2, then from −2 to 2, for distance 2+4.

questions.prompt: Two coordinate systems describe the same straight-line motion with positions r(t)=s(t)+10 meters. Which statement is correct wherever s is twice differentiable?
options: The velocities and accelerations are equal in both coordinate systems.
The velocity described by r exceeds that of s by 10 m/s.
The acceleration described by r exceeds that of s by 10 m/s².
The speed in the r system is always 10 m/s.
questions.explanation: Differentiating r=s+10 gives r′=s′ and r″=s″. Thus velocity, acceleration and speed are unchanged by a fixed shift of the coordinate origin. The positions themselves differ, but their time increments are identical. A: The constant position offset has zero first and second derivatives. B: A constant position offset is not a velocity offset. C: Differentiating a constant twice still gives zero. D: Changing the coordinate origin does not prescribe a constant speed.
